title: The Clay Jar Treasure Bible
summary: The Bible in clear, everyday English, written thought for thought so that anyone can understand it. This page tells you about the name, the copyright, how we write, and where the text comes from.

items.label: Style
items.value: Thought for thought, in plain English

items.label: Scope
items.value: Old Testament, Apocrypha, New Testament, Pseudepigrapha

blocks.text: In a letter to the church in Corinth, the apostle Paul said that we carry a treasure in plain clay jars (2 Corinthians 4:7). The treasure is God’s message. The jar is just the container. This Bible tries to be a clear, simple jar, so that the treasure is easy to see and to understand.
It is the family edition of the Clay Jar Translation, a separate word-for-word Bible that is in the public domain.
The text, footnotes, headings, and introductions of the Clay Jar Treasure Bible are copyrighted. They were written fresh for this Bible and are not copied from any other copyrighted work.
Free to read. You can read this Bible online and offline, with no sign-up, no ads, and no tracking.

Quoting. You may quote up to 500 verses of the Clay Jar Treasure Bible in print, online, or in a talk or song, as long as you give credit, for example “Scripture quotations are from the Clay Jar Treasure Bible, © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.” For anything more, please ask first.
The Clay Jar Translation (CJT) is a different book. Its text is in the public domain, and you can find it at clayjartranslation.github.io.

Holy God, Maker of heaven and earth, you spoke and light came into being, and you formed us from the dust and breathed your life into us. We come to you now as clay in the hands of the potter. We ask you to guide this work of translation. Open our eyes to see what your word truly says, and give us humility to set aside what we wish it said. Where the old manuscripts speak with one voice, help us to carry their words faithfully; where they differ, give us patience, honesty, and wisdom to weigh them well.

Guard us from pride, from carelessness, and from adding to or taking away from your words. Send your Spirit, who first moved over the waters, to move over our minds and our hands as we work. Let every page we make be clear, true, and free, so that people who have never held a Bible, and people who have read it all their lives, may find you in it. Bless Jose and everyone who will read, check, correct, and share this translation. We offer it back to you, for it was always yours. In your holy name we pray. Amen.

steps.title: Thought for thought
steps.detail: We ask what the Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek author meant, and then we say that in clear English. We do not follow the word order of the old languages.

steps.title: Short, common words
steps.detail: Short sentences and everyday words, so that a reader about ten or eleven years old can follow. Hard church words are explained instead of used as labels. For example, “made right with God” is used instead of “justified”, and the older word is in a footnote.

steps.title: Faithful to the meaning
steps.detail: We do not add ideas or leave any out. Where the old manuscripts differ in an important way, a footnote says so.

steps.title: Poetry stays poetry
steps.detail: Psalms, proverbs, and prophets are set in lines, and the headings over each section are written fresh for this Bible.

steps.title: Names, measures, and times
steps.detail: God’s name YHWH is Yahweh. Compound names of God, like El Shaddai, are kept in their original form, and names of God, people, and places are explained in a footnote at first mention. Distances, weights, money, months, and clock times are given in the way we use them today, with the original in a footnote.

steps.title: Few, simple footnotes
steps.detail: Footnotes are kept for important manuscript differences and for the meanings of names.

blocks.text: We start from the oldest witnesses we have: the Hebrew text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint (the early Greek Old Testament), the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the oldest Greek manuscripts and papyri of the New Testament. Our own word-for-word public-domain work, the Clay Jar Translation, helps us keep the meaning exact. We never copy wording from any copyrighted English Bible.

blocks.text: This Bible is being written book by book, in the order of the Old Testament, the Apocrypha, the New Testament, and then the Pseudepigrapha. The home page shows which chapters are ready. Books are grouped by tradition, not by authority: the Apocrypha are accepted as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches, and the Pseudepigrapha are included for study.

sections.heading: An honest note on this draft

blocks.text: This is a draft. It is written with AI assistance and has not yet been checked by scholars. Every chapter is compared with many modern Bibles by computer, and any wording that is too close to a copyrighted Bible is rewritten. Please tell us about any mistakes.
